title: Know the fire before the alarm
allegory: A threat model and spec are like planning a smoke alarm: you first picture the fire you fear and how it spreads, place the detector at the step where it can still be caught, decide exactly what reading counts, and wire the alarm to what everyone does next.
map: the fire you fear, told as a story: pan left on, smoke, flames, the house
the threat model: a causal chain from a model capability to real harm, with assumptions at each step
the step where the fire can still be caught: the smoke
the step in the chain that a model capability actually gates
'this much smoke, for this long' counts as a fire
the operational definition: the exact experiment and what counts as a matching answer
the alarm is wired to 'everyone out'
a threshold written in advance, tied to a decision: ship, don't ship, ship with mitigations
smoke, heat and gas detectors together, so burnt toast can't decide
several operational definitions per property, avoiding mono-metric bias

chapters.name: A number, then shrugs
chapters.note: a score with no line is just a number

cap.1: You build a careful test, the model scores 62%, and the room goes quiet. Is that bad? Should anyone act? Nobody knows, because nobody said beforehand.
cap.2: An eval with no threat model has no threshold, so its score is just a number. ARENA names this failure: the questions may measure the property, but nothing ties it to a harm or a decision.
cap.3: Without a pre-registered link from property to harm, a result can't bind a decision, and one operational definition quietly stands in for the whole property: mono-metric bias.

cap.1: A smoke alarm works because someone first pictured the fire: pan left on, then smoke, then flames. The alarm sits at the smoke, early enough to act.
cap.2: A threat model is that picture for AI: a causal chain from a model capability to real harm, naming who has what access at each step. Then find the one step the capability actually gates.
cap.3: Threat model: a causal graph whose nodes are claims or events and whose edges are causal links, with assumptions about capability, access and deployment named. It answers 'what should I evaluate?'

cap.1: Now pin the fuzzy word. Not 'dangerous', but a narrow definition, a test you could actually run, and the result that would change what you do.
cap.2: The spec narrows the property, lists the axes it varies along, then operationalises it: the exact experiment and what counts as a match. Then check backwards: does a high score bring the harm closer?
cap.3: Specification: narrowed definition, optional subproperties, axes of variation, severity milestones; then an operational definition measuring part of the property. Every operational definition undershoots it.

chapters.name: The line, drawn first
chapters.title: May 2025: bio evals against a threshold written in advance

cap.1: In May 2025 Anthropic's bioweapons tests came back murky for Claude Opus 4. The line was drawn in advance, so murky meant: ship with heavier safety controls.
cap.2: Anthropic couldn't clearly rule out ASL-3 risks for Opus 4, so it shipped under the ASL-3 Standard. The same evals ruled out ASL-4 for Opus 4 and ASL-3 for Sonnet 4: the suite discriminated fine.
cap.3: The useful output isn't a point estimate but which side of a pre-registered line the result fails to clear. A threshold written first turns ambiguity into a precautionary action, not a debate.

chapters.name: Toast sets it off
chapters.verdict: Every operational definition undershoots the property, so write more than one.

cap.1: A smoke-only alarm shrieks at burnt toast and sleeps through a gas leak. One test fires on the wrong thing and misses the right one.
cap.2: Letting one operational definition stand in for a whole property is mono-metric bias: it can measure the prompt rather than the property, and misses parts of it. The fix: two or three definitions.
cap.3: ARENA's sycophancy example: the rate of flipping a correct answer after a user challenge, with the reverse flip as a control for ordinary corrigibility. Each definition measures only part of the property.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Name the decision the number feeds
Two or three definitions, not one

cap.1: Tests only help steer AI when you know what a result would make you do. Draw the line first, then measure, and even a murky result tells you how to act.
cap.2: Everything downstream inherits this: dataset generation, Inspect scoring and agent evals. If you can't name the decision the number feeds, you're not ready to build the eval.
cap.3: Each eval is evidence in a safety case, a structured argument that a system is unlikely to cause catastrophe. AI control is the mirror image: which protocol keeps us safe, not which number says we need one.

coda.title: Toy decision rule: where does the eval's range sit against the line you drew first?

readouts.label: can you rule out crossing the line?
readouts.f: m + w < 60 ? 'yes: even the high end is below it' : 'no'

readouts.label: decision, written in advance
readouts.f: m + w < 60 ? 'ship with standard protections' : (m - w >= 60 ? 'crossed: stronger protections required' : 'cannot rule out: ship with stronger protections anyway')

caption.1: Slide the best guess and the uncertainty. If even the high end stays under the line, the risk is ruled out. If the range straddles it, act as if it's crossed.
caption.2: The line and the actions were fixed before the eval ran, so every result maps to a decision. Anthropic's Opus 4 call was the straddling case: ASL-3 risks couldn't be ruled out, so it shipped under ASL-3.
caption.3: A decision rule on an interval, not a point: rule out only if the upper bound clears the threshold. Wide uncertainty makes precaution the default; better evals narrow the band and discriminate.

where_else: Medical screening: fix the disease, the marker and the cut-off before reading any result
Safety cases: each eval is one piece of evidence in a structured argument
AI control: the mirror question, which protocol keeps us safe once the number says we need one
Software alerting: an alert is only useful when it is tied to a harm and a runbook

hamming.what: A written causal story from a model capability to real harm, plus a narrow, measurable definition of that capability and the result that would change a decision.
hamming.when: Before writing a single eval question, whenever a number is meant to inform shipping, mitigations or research priorities.
hamming.why: Without it an eval measures the prompt rather than the property, and even a clean score can't tell anyone what to do.

object.title: The detector board
object.subtitle: three detectors, three events: what each one catches

cap.1: One detector, smoke only. It catches the pan fire, but it also shrieks at burnt toast and sleeps through a gas leak.
cap.2: One operational definition standing in for the whole property 'danger in the kitchen'. It fires on an artefact (toast) and misses part of the property (gas): mono-metric bias.
cap.3: An operational definition both overshoots, firing on artefacts of the measurement, and undershoots, missing parts of the property it can't see. A single metric hides both.

cap.1: Add a heat detector. The pan fire now trips two detectors and the toast only one: you can start telling a real fire from breakfast.
cap.2: A second definition with different blind spots lets you check agreement: a real effect should show up under both, an artefact under only one.
cap.3: Convergent evidence from operational definitions with different failure modes is what licenses a claim about the underlying property rather than about one test.

cap.1: Add a gas detector and the leak is covered too. Three imperfect detectors cover the danger better than one polished one.
cap.2: Two or three operational definitions per property, so no single measurement artefact carries the whole claim. Decomposing the property tells you which ones you need.
cap.3: Coverage of the threat model's gating steps matters more than any one metric's polish; subproperties and axes of variation say where the coverage gaps are.

cap.1: From above, see which dangers the board covers. You could only lay out this board because someone first wrote down the fires and leaks they feared.
cap.2: The columns come from the threat model: the harms you listed decide which detectors you need. No harm story, no columns, and no way to see what's missing.
cap.3: The threat model defines the target set. Without it, coverage is undefined, and a high score on one metric can't be read as evidence for or against the harm.

predict.q: Only the smoke detector is on, and burnt toast sets it off. What went wrong?

options.t: it fired on something that isn't the harm

predict.why: The test caught an artefact rather than the property, like an eval that measures the prompt rather than the property.

predict.q: Which danger does the smoke detector alone miss?
predict.why: A gas leak makes no smoke. One operational definition always leaves part of the property unseen.

predict.q: Before choosing any detector, what should you write down first?

options.t: which harms you fear and how they unfold

predict.why: The threat model decides what to measure; the specification then decides how.

object.where: Any test that must trigger an action: medical screening cut-offs, factory quality checks, alerting on a production system.
